dsa5101-frequent-itemsets.title: Association-rule reasoning studio
dsa5101-frequent-itemsets.learningGoal: Separate counting baskets, pruning candidates, and interpreting a rule's conditional strength.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: The lecture and assignment establish the calculation workflow; MMDS provides the full frequent-itemset chapter as labeled depth.

exercises.label: Support
exercises.prompt: How does a basket table become a support value?
exercises.takeaway: Count qualifying transactions first; normalize only after the numerator is explicit.
steps: Identify the baskets containing every item in the candidate.
Divide by the total number of transactions.
Use downward closure to remove every superset safely.
Only after frequent sets are known should rule confidence be interpreted.

exercises.label: Confidence
exercises.prompt: Why is the antecedent the denominator?
exercises.takeaway: Confidence is conditional: among baskets with A, how often does B also occur?
steps: Start with the baskets that already contain the antecedent.
The denominator is the antecedent support, not all baskets.
A high conditional rate can still add little information when B is common.

exercises.label: Interest
exercises.prompt: What does a base-rate comparison add?
exercises.takeaway: Lift or interest asks whether the consequent is more likely than its background frequency.
steps: Measure how common the consequent is without conditioning.
Measure how common B is among A baskets.
A value above one indicates positive association under this measure.
A rule can be predictive without proving that A causes B.

dsa5101-frequent-itemsets.explanation: Each tab isolates a different denominator or interpretation so support, confidence, and lift do not blur together.

animation.title: The basket detective
animation.analogy: Imagine checking lunch baskets to find snacks that often travel together.

frames.label: 1 · Look
frames.scene: Mark every basket that contains both snacks.
frames.takeaway: Support is a count of baskets, not a feeling about popularity.

frames.label: 2 · Prune
frames.scene: If a smaller snack pair is already rare, cross out every larger basket pattern that contains it.
frames.takeaway: Downward closure saves work before the big search.

frames.label: 3 · Ask
frames.scene: Now ask whether the second snack appears more often after the first snack.
frames.takeaway: Confidence is conditional; lift compares with the background rate.

dsa5101-minhash-lsh.title: MinHash-to-LSH trace
dsa5101-minhash-lsh.learningGoal: Follow the chain from set similarity to compact signatures and then to candidate generation.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: The assignment requires the probability calculation; MMDS supplies the derivation and parameter trade-off as textbook depth.

steps: Define similarity before choosing a sketch.
A collision is an unbiased similarity signal under a random permutation.
At least one matching band is enough to pass the candidate filter.
LSH generates candidates; it does not certify every candidate as a true neighbor.
dsa5101-minhash-lsh.explanation: The trace keeps exact similarity, compact estimation, and approximate candidate retrieval as three different operations.

animation.title: The sticker-album shortcut
animation.analogy: Two sticker albums can be compared quickly without laying every sticker on the floor.

frames.label: 1 · Albums
frames.scene: Treat each document as an album of stickers called shingles.
frames.takeaway: Jaccard similarity asks how much the albums overlap.

frames.label: 2 · Tiny signature
frames.scene: Shuffle the sticker rows and keep the first sticker seen for each shuffle.
frames.takeaway: Matching MinHash entries estimate the overlap.

frames.label: 3 · Candidate bell
frames.scene: Put signature rows into bands; a matching band rings a bell for a possible neighbor.
frames.takeaway: LSH proposes candidates; exact verification still checks the real sets.

splits.label: Rank nodes by link structure

dsa5101-ranking-streams.explanation: The right method follows the target quantity: node importance, a recent-window count, or distinct-cardinality estimation.

animation.title: The toy-box organizer
animation.analogy: Put similar toys together, then check whether the boxes still tell the truth when the toy room grows huge.

frames.label: 1 · Nearby toys
frames.scene: Give each toy to the closest box or join boxes using a chosen linkage rule.
frames.takeaway: The distance and geometry decide what “similar” means.

frames.label: 2 · Move the label
frames.scene: For K-means, move each box label to the mean position of its toys and repeat.
frames.takeaway: Each update improves the local squared-error objective, but initialization can still matter.

frames.label: 3 · Tiny summary
frames.scene: Keep confident toys in DS, uncertain groups in CS, and lonely outliers in RS; CURE keeps several boundary representatives.
frames.takeaway: BFR and CURE trade exact detail for a compact, auditable summary.

frames.label: 4 · Check
frames.scene: Count how many toys land in the right labelled box, but also ask whether the boxes are useful and not just tiny.
frames.takeaway: Purity alone is not a complete quality claim.

animation.title: The movie-buddy club
animation.analogy: Find friends with similar taste, but also learn a compact taste profile so the two methods do not get mixed up.

frames.label: 1 · Center
frames.scene: Subtract each friend’s usual star level so “generous rater” does not look like “same taste.”
frames.takeaway: Mean-centering compares patterns of likes and dislikes.

frames.label: 2 · Borrow
frames.scene: Let nearby taste-buddies vote on the missing movie rating.
frames.takeaway: User-based filtering is a neighborhood calculation.

frames.label: 3 · Learn
frames.scene: Give each friend and movie a tiny hidden taste vector, then combine matching coordinates.
frames.takeaway: Latent factors predict with a dot product, a different model path.

animation.title: The bouncing web ball
animation.analogy: A ball visits web pages, shares its weight along links, and sometimes jumps to a chosen page.

frames.label: 1 · Share
frames.scene: A page with two outgoing links splits its ball weight between the two destinations.
frames.takeaway: Fix row-versus-column orientation before multiplying.

frames.label: 2 · Jump
frames.scene: A small teleport jump prevents the ball from getting trapped in a corner of the web.
frames.takeaway: Damping mixes link-following with teleportation.

frames.label: 3 · Repeat
frames.scene: Repeat the sharing until the page weights settle into a stable pattern.
frames.takeaway: Power iteration is a repeated state update; dangling pages need a convention.

animation.title: The tiny notebook
animation.analogy: A stream is a never-ending parade, so the notebook keeps only a clever summary instead of every visitor.

frames.label: 1 · Recent window
frames.scene: DGIM groups recent 1s into timestamped buckets and keeps at most two buckets of each size.
frames.takeaway: The oldest partly covered bucket explains the count error.

frames.label: 2 · New names
frames.scene: Flajolet–Martin watches the longest run of zeroes in hashed names.
frames.takeaway: It estimates distinct items, not a recent-window count.

frames.label: 3 · Repeated visits
frames.scene: AMS samples positions to estimate how strongly repeated values dominate the parade.
frames.takeaway: The second moment squares frequencies, so it is a different target.

animation.title: The two toy shops
animation.analogy: Two shops have limited coins; each new toy request must be sent to an eligible shop.

frames.label: 1 · Check
frames.scene: Write down which shops bid for this toy and how many coins each shop has left.
frames.takeaway: The state is the remaining budget, not just the current request.

frames.label: 2 · Choose
frames.scene: Give the toy to the eligible shop with more coins left; make the tie rule explicit.
frames.takeaway: BALANCE is a local choice that must be traced step by step.

frames.label: 3 · Challenge
frames.scene: Try a different request order and see whether a lucky run still proves a guarantee.
frames.takeaway: One successful sequence is not a proof of optimality.
